name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
title: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
answer: Fabricated citations and fact checking concerns the detection and prevention of references that do not exist, misattribute sources, or misrepresent what a source says. It covers scholarly publishing, legal filings, journalism, and AI-generated text where language models can produce plausible but false bibliographic entries. The scope includes both manual editorial review and automated tools that compare a citation against databases, publisher pages, or the original paper. It also extends to verifying factual claims extracted from research, not just the presence of a DOI or title.

sections.body: Fabricated citations and fact checking concerns the detection and prevention of references that do not exist, misattribute sources, or misrepresent what a source says. It covers scholarly publishing, legal filings, journalism, and AI-generated text where language models can produce plausible but false bibliographic entries. The scope includes both manual editorial review and automated tools that compare a citation against databases, publisher pages, or the original paper. It also extends to verifying factual claims extracted from research, not just the presence of a DOI or title.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on bibliographic databases, full-text repositories, and metadata services that allow a citation to be resolved to a real record. Automated systems often use retrieval pipelines that query Crossref, PubMed, or institutional catalogues, then compare the returned metadata with the cited string. For fact checking claims, the infrastructure includes document stores of research papers and extracted claim sets, such as the 11,222 claims held in this site's library, which can be matched against source text. Compute is modest compared to training large models, since most checks are search and string or embedding comparison tasks.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by breaking a citation into fields such as author, title, journal, volume, and year, then querying authoritative indexes for a matching record. When no record is found, the citation is flagged as likely fabricated; when a record exists, the next step is to check that the cited page or section actually supports the claim attributed to it. Fact checking extracted claims uses retrieval augmented verification, where a claim is encoded and compared against candidate passages from the original paper. Human reviewers then adjudicate borderline cases, because a real citation can still be used misleadingly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here center on provenance, accountability, and the harm caused by false authority. A fabricated citation can pollute the scholarly record, mislead courts or clinicians, and erode trust in AI-assisted writing. Institutions and publishers increasingly require authors to disclose AI use and to verify every reference against the original source, not a secondary summary. Provenance is maintained by linking claims and citations to the original paper, which is why this site does not link to the Consensus search tool but to the source document itself. There is also a risk of over-flagging, where an automated checker marks a real but poorly indexed citation as fake, so human review remains part of responsible practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward verification at the moment of generation, where writing assistants check each citation before it appears in a draft. Shared registries of retracted or fabricated references may become more common, allowing publishers and courts to screen submissions quickly. Better models for claim entailment will reduce the gap between checking that a citation exists and checking that it supports the sentence it is attached to. Over time, fact checking may become a standard layer in research workflows rather than a separate cleanup step.
